research_analysis.exact_observed_hook: "You could rebrand anything to sound healthy, but how easy would it be to do the opposite and rebrand blueberries to sound unhealthy?"
research_analysis.visual_hook: A man in glasses and a black t-shirt at a white desk with a clear clamshell of fresh blueberries in front of him, studio wall and neon sign behind.
research_analysis.narrative_structure: A reverse-premise question, 'Let's find out', then a step-by-step build where each choice (container, name, mascot, tagline, background) is explained in one line while the product mockup changes on the desk, then the final reveal and a 'what should I rebrand next' prompt.
research_analysis.viral_mechanism: The viewer watches a product change in stages and wants to see the finished object. Each step is a small design decision with a stated reason, so the entertainment doubles as a lesson without a lecture.
research_analysis.observed_evidence: 4.6M views, 62.4x the creator's 73.8K median, 100s, 512.5K followers. The mockup evolves on the desk through the video. Series prompt in the close. The original relies on custom illustration and motion graphics.
research_analysis.performance_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the before/after object is the retention device, and asking what to rebrand next generates comments that double as a content queue. Viewers send it to a friend with the invented product name.
research_analysis.why_this_format_fits_alex: It demonstrates what his agency sells (framing changes perceived value) on a three-dollar object, with a result anyone can judge on sight. His time in France gives him a real reason for the French name, and Canva keeps it inside his skills.
research_analysis.originality_changes: Borrowed: 'can I rebrand X to sound like the opposite', staged build on a desk, series question at the end. New: the product, the direction (cheap to luxury, played for comedy), every name and line, no mascot or illustration, and a cut to about 45 seconds.

alex_adaptation.concept: Alex puts a real gas station hot dog on his desk and upgrades it in four moves, each a real pricing or menu-design choice: a French name, a serif font with lots of empty space, a description that is technically true, and a price with no dollar sign. The reveal is the same hot dog on a white plate next to a printed menu card.
alex_adaptation.target_audience: People who like watching something get transformed; restaurant and small-business owners; anyone who has overpaid for a small plate.
alex_adaptation.primary_emotion: Amusement, then 'wait, that would actually work on me'
alex_adaptation.first_frame: A gas station hot dog in its paper tray sitting alone in the middle of a clean desk, Alex behind it with his hands flat on the table, looking at it with respect.
alex_adaptation.first_spoken_line: This is a gas station hot dog. Give me four changes in Canva and I'll make you want to pay fourteen dollars for it.

full_script.speaker: Alex
full_script.dialogue: One. The name. I lived in France for a while, so I'm allowed to do this. It's now Le Chien Chaud. Which is just 'the hot dog'. In French. That's twelve dollars right there.
full_script.action: Says 'Le Chien Chaud' with total commitment and a real accent, one hand doing a small chef's flourish. Drops back to normal voice for 'which is just the hot dog'.
full_script.camera: Cut to laptop screen recording: blank Canva page, he types the name
full_script.editing: Picture-in-picture: his face small in the corner over the Canva recording

full_script.speaker: Alex
full_script.dialogue: Two. The font. Thin, serif, and way too much empty space around it. Empty space is how a menu tells you it's expensive.
full_script.action: In the corner inset he squints approvingly at the screen.
full_script.camera: Screen recording: he changes the font to a thin serif, shrinks it, drags it to the center of a mostly empty page
full_script.on_screen_text: 2. THE FONT → more nothing = more money

full_script.speaker: Alex
full_script.dialogue: Three. The description. 'Slow-turned for six hours.' Which is true. It was on the roller since this morning.
full_script.action: Deadpan on 'which is true'. Tiny pause before 'since this morning'.
full_script.camera: Screen recording: he types the description in small italics under the name
full_script.on_screen_text: 3. THE DESCRIPTION → slow-turned for six hours
full_script.editing: Normal speed for the typing so the line can be read

full_script.speaker: Alex
full_script.dialogue: Four. The price. No dollar sign. No cents. Just 'fourteen'. A dollar sign reminds you it's money.
full_script.action: Holds up four fingers, then mimes plucking a dollar sign out of the air and flicking it away.
full_script.camera: Back to the desk shot. He holds the printed card up beside his face.

alternate_hooks: I paid a couple dollars for this hot dog. Watch me turn it into a fourteen-dollar menu item without touching the food.
Restaurants do four things to make you pay more. I'm going to do all four to a gas station hot dog.
I lived in France. I'm about to misuse that.
alternate_endings: After the reveal he slides the plate toward the lens: 'You'd order it. Don't lie.' Cut.
After the reveal: text only, 'the hot dog did not change. you did.' while he eats it in silence.

alex_adaptation.call_to_action: 'What should I make expensive next?' The comments become the series queue.

props: One gas station hot dog in its paper tray
One printed menu card (home printer or a pharmacy print for under a dollar), folded to stand
production.wardrobe: Plain dark t-shirt; optional: a kitchen towel over one shoulder for the reveal
shot_list: Desk shot: intro with hot dog in tray
Desk shot: price line with printed card
b_roll: Buying the hot dog at the station (exterior and roller grill only, no staff)
production.editor_instructions: Build the card in Canva on a white page: name in a thin serif at about 28 pt, description in 10 pt italics, price as the number alone, everything centered with wide margins. Record the screen while building it so the steps are real. Replace the {{REAL}} token with the price on his receipt. Keep each numbered text card in the same top-left position. The four reasons are common menu-design practice stated as his view; do not add statistics. Only say 'on the roller since this morning' if he bought it in the afternoon; otherwise use 'slow-turned for hours'. Cut anything that pushes it past 48 seconds.

variants_to_test: Alternate hook: 'I lived in France. I'm about to misuse that.'
Alternate payoff: 'You'd order it. Don't lie.'
testing.promotion_decision: Brand fit 3: promote at 48h if views are at least 3x his trailing median and either follows or shares per 1,000 reached is top quartile; if comments are full of 'do X next', film the top request within 72 hours as the sequel.
follow_up_variations_if_successful: The most-requested item from the comments, same four moves
Reverse: make a nice restaurant's dish sound like a gas station item with the same four levers pushed the other way
A local business's real flyer, redone with the four moves, with the owner's permission

creative_confidence.score_type: Subjective production-priority score, not predicted viral probability
creative_confidence.rationale: A visible transformation with a real reveal, his France background used for a joke, and a built-in series question. It shows what his agency does on an object everyone understands. It is a 46-second multi-shot edit, longer and more work than his proven formats.
uncertainties: One {{REAL}} token: the hot dog's price
The 'six hours' line must be true or be swapped for the safer wording
Menu-design reasons are presented as his view, not as cited research
Length and edit load are outside his proven range
His French pronunciation needs to be good enough to be funny on purpose
